§CH01§ Trick number one. Make it flat. A chicken breast is fat on one end and thin on the
SHOTS.name: make it flat

SHOTS.txt: teardrop. So by the time the fat end is cooked, the
thin end is shoe leather. That's why your chicken's dry. It's
not the oven, and it's not you. So put the breast in a
zip bag, or between two pieces of plastic wrap. And take a
rolling pin, or a heavy can of beans, or the bottom of a little
skillet, and pound the thick end, gently, till the whole
thing is the same thickness. About three quarters of an inch. Like
this. You're not trying to flatten it like a pancake. You're just
evening it out. Start in the middle of the thick
part and work out toward the edge.
Harold used to come in from the garage when he heard me doing this. He thought
I was hammering on the cabinets. I told him, I'm tenderizing
your supper, go sit down. Now look.
Same thickness from one end to the other. It
cooks evenly, so no end is dry. That one
trick fixes half the dry chicken in America. And the
bag keeps everything clean, so there's no raw chicken splashed on your
counter. When you're done, the bag goes right in the trash.
Trick number two. Salt it ahead. Fifteen minutes is all you need. Put two
SHOTS.name: salt it ahead

SHOTS.txt: cups of cold water in a bowl and stir in one
tablespoon of salt till it's gone. Put the chicken
breast in that, and set it in the refrigerator for fifteen minutes.
Not longer than an hour, or it gets too salty. The
salt water gets into the meat and helps it hold on
to its own juice while it cooks. It's the same
reason my mother soaked the Thanksgiving turkey in a washtub of salt water
in the cold back porch, the night before. She didn't know why it
worked. She just knew the turkey was never dry. If you don't want to
fuss with water, just sprinkle half a teaspoon of salt on both sides
and let it sit on a plate in the refrigerator for thirty minutes.
Same idea. That's what I do most nights. I salt
it when I put the kettle on, and by the time I've had my tea, it's ready.
